content: Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea (CDAD) has been observed with the use of nearly all antibacterial agents, including fosfomycin (MONUROL). The severity of CDAD can vary, ranging from mild diarrhea to life-threatening colitis. The use of antibacterial agents disrupts the normal microbial flora of the colon, which can lead to an overgrowth of Clostridium difficile. Clostridium difficile produces two toxins, toxin A and toxin B, which are responsible for the development of CDAD. Strains of C. difficile that produce hypertoxins are associated with higher rates of morbidity and mortality. These infections are often resistant to standard antimicrobial treatments and, in severe cases, may necessitate surgical intervention, such as colectomy. CDAD should be considered as a potential diagnosis in any patient who develops diarrhea after the use of antibiotics. A thorough medical history is essential, as CDAD has been reported to occur even up to two months after the completion of antibiotic therapy. If CDAD is suspected or confirmed, it may be necessary to discontinue the use of the current antibiotic regimen if it is not specifically targeting C. difficile. difficile, and surgical evaluation when clinically warranted.
